description.value: The study used fMRI and Dependency Network Analysis to examine influence hierarchies within and between emotional reactivity and regulation networks during high- and low-anger periods of a movie.

value: we therefore hypothesized that the reported increase in anger intensity would involve modulations in connectivity within and between neural networks that are implicated in emotion reactivity (including the insula and the amygdala), and executive control (including IFG and MiFG; Hypothesis 1).

Furthermore, the vmPFC which is considered a major player in the implicit emotional regulation network (Etkin et al.,  2015 ) is expected to be particularly influential on network organization during high anger moments (Hypothesis 2).

Lastly, difference in network hierarchy between the anger conditions was expected to correlate with both self-reported angry feelings during the movie (i.e., anger state) and anger and emotional regulation tendencies (i.e., anger trait; Hypothesis 3).

value: The vmPFC had significantly higher influence on both the emotional reactivity and regulation networks in the high anger condition compared with the low anger condition.

The vmPFC was identified as a central node during the high anger episode based on its impact on whole-system connectivity, and its influence may reflect a process aimed at exerting control over anger stemming from the provocation.

spans.text: D NA identified the vmPFC regulation-related region as a central node during the high anger episode based on its impact both on whole system connectivity, and on intra- and inter network connectivity.

model_representation_notes.value: Dependency Network Analysis estimates an influence hierarchy from correlation and partial-correlation dependencies; it does not establish true causal influence. The high- and low-anger periods were epochs of a naturalistic movie and may also differ in perceptual features unrelated to emotion.

spans.text: It should also be noted that while D NA can be used to make inferences regarding the influence hierarchy within a network, it does not infer a causal influence in the true sense, as correlation does not imply causation (Friston,  2009 ).

source_definition.value: Anger period was defined from continuous retrospective anger ratings as two equal-length 132-second movie epochs: a high-anger period from 195–327 seconds and a low-anger period from 36–168 seconds.

spans.text: This procedure yielded a unique solution of two intervals of 132 s in which the median anger rating across all participants reached its maximum (195–327 s; hereby termed high-anger period), and minimum (36–168 s; hereby termed low-anger period).

model_settings.value: Dependency Network Analysis used Pearson ROI-ROI correlations followed by Fisher Z transformation, partial correlations, nonnegative influence values with negative values reset to zero, and dependency/influencing-degree sums. Analyses compared equal-length 132-second high- and low-anger epochs using paired t-tests, with FDR correction for multiple comparisons.

estimator.value: Pearson correlation, partial correlation, and paired t-test

spans.text: ROI-ROI correlations were calculated by Pearson’s formula
